2.text: Reindeer Chukchee, however, the chief articles of value used for exchange

3.text: are fawn-skins gathered in spring and summer. Such skins will, of course,

4.text: be in the possession of the master only, with the exception of a very few,

5.text: which the assistant may have from his own reindeer. Therefore the master,

6.text: after coming from a trading-place, will take some part of the wares brought

7.text: home, and give to his assistants, especially if they were not successful in the

8.text: hunt, and thus were short of means for making purchases. In the course of

9.text: time the master will give to his assistants some of his tea and tobacco, when

10.text: they have none; at least, a master who is “good” will act thus.

11.text: Not rarely is it the case that a family whose prosperity has declined,

12.text: and whose herd is not large enough to provide for their subsistence, prefers,

13.text: instead of continuing a half-hungry life, to join the camp of some rich rein-

14.text: deer-breeder short of hands. Of course, rich owners sometimes have misgivings

15.text: regarding such impoverished neighbors, fearing that the bad luck of their herd

16.text: may prove detrimental to their own prosperity.¹ Still the need of extra herds-

17.text: men is often stronger than such fear; especially when the poorer family, after

18.text: losing a part of their herds, has succeeded in allaying the misfortune and in

19.text: remaining for some years in circumstances not utterly hopeless.

20.text: In combinations where large and small herds are joined together, the

21.text: families of new assistants receive only a part of their subsistence from the

22.text: master, and take another portion from their own herd. At each slaughtering

23.text: the herdsmen slaughter such animals as the master points out, and carry them

24.text: to the entrance of such and such a house, according to his order; then, if

25.text: some house is left without an animal, the people catch one of their own

26.text: reindeer and slaughter it. In this case, however, the connection between

27.text: master and assistant is not very strong, and may in a short time be dissolved.

28.text: On the contrary, typical assistants receive from their masters, besides the

29.text: food, also a few live fawns, as a yearly present. In the latter part of the

30.text: summer the fawns are marked on the ear with the mark of the proprietor.

31.text: When a fawn is caught and handed over to the master, the latter sometimes,

32.text: instead of biting² into its ear the lines of his own mark, tenders it to one of

33.text: the assistants, and says briefly, g̣ɪnaˊn (“yourself”). Then the animal is marked

34.text: by the assistant, and belongs to him. The number of such animals depends

35.text: on the size of the herd, and still more on the mortality among the fawns

36.text: during the preceding spring. In a good year an assistant may receive from

37.text: the master three, five, and even more animals. These grow up in the

38.text: common herd of the camp, and all the increase belongs also to the assistant.

39.text: I have mentioned before that under favorable circumstances reindeer multiply

40.text: very fast, since the doe bears fawns even from the very first year. At the

41.text: next slaughtering the master will always consent to slaughter a young buck

43.text: ² Regarding the process of marking animals by biting them in the ear, cf. p. 84.
